questions.q: Light travels in
questions.explain: Light travels in straight lines through one material. This is why light is drawn as straight rays with arrows.
questions.lo: State that light travels in straight lines, shown as rays with arrows

notes.0: Light does not curve as it travels through one material. It only changes direction when it hits a surface or enters a different material.
notes.1: Light spreads out from a source in all directions, but each ray does not go round in a circle. Think about the shape of a ray in a ray diagram.
notes.3: A zigzag path would mean light keeps changing direction on its own. In one material nothing makes light change direction, so think about the shape of its path.

why.right: Shadows have sharp edges because light cannot bend around an object in its path.
wrong: Shadows have sharp edges because objects absorb light and give out darkness.
Shadows have sharp edges because light slows down when it passes an object.

questions.q: In a ray diagram, the arrow on a ray shows the
questions.explain: The arrow on a ray shows the direction in which light travels, from the source towards where the light goes.
questions.lo: State that light travels in straight lines, shown as rays with arrows

notes.1: A ray diagram does not show how fast light moves. The arrowhead points one way along the ray, so think about what that tells you about the light.
notes.2: Colour is not shown by the arrowhead on a ray. The arrow points one way along the line, so think about what that tells you about the light.
notes.3: Brightness is not shown by an arrowhead. The arrow points one way along the ray, so think about what that tells you about the path of the light.

questions.q: One card in a row of holed cards is moved. Why is the flame now hidden?
questions.explain: Light travels in straight lines. When one card is moved, its hole is no longer in line with the others, so the light from the flame is blocked.
questions.lo: State that light travels in straight lines, shown as rays with arrows

notes.0: The flame still gives out light when a card is moved. What has changed is the path to the eye, so think about how the holes need to be lined up.
notes.1: If light travelled in curves, it could pass through holes that are out of line. The flame is hidden, so think about what that shows about the path of light.
notes.2: If light bent around cards, the flame would still be seen after a card is moved. The flame is hidden, so light cannot get around the card.

why.right: The flame is hidden because light cannot follow a curved path through holes that are out of line.
wrong: The flame is hidden because light curves away from any card that has been moved.
The flame is hidden because light becomes too weak after passing through a moved card.

questions.q: A luminous object is one that
choices: can only be seen in the dark
questions.explain: A luminous object gives out its own light, for example the sun, a candle flame or a switched-on lamp.
questions.lo: Classify objects as luminous or non-luminous

notes.0: Luminous objects can be seen in daylight too, such as the sun. Being luminous is about where the light of the object comes from, not when it is seen.
notes.2: An object that only reflects light from other things is non-luminous, like the moon. Think about whether the light starts in the object itself.
notes.3: An object that absorbs all light gives out no light, so it looks black. Think about objects that are a source of light.

questions.q: Which object is luminous?
questions.explain: A firefly produces its own light, so it is luminous. The mirror, the moon and the flower are seen only because they reflect light.
questions.lo: Classify objects as luminous or non-luminous

notes.1: A mirror looks bright only because it reflects light from other sources. In the dark it gives out no light of its own.
notes.2: The moon shines only because it reflects sunlight. It does not produce any light of its own.
notes.3: A white flower reflects most of the light falling on it, which makes it look bright. It does not produce light itself.

why.right: A firefly is luminous because it produces light inside its own body.
wrong: A firefly is luminous because it reflects moonlight more strongly than other objects.
A firefly is luminous because it stores sunlight in the day and releases it at night.

questions.q: Which object is non-luminous?
questions.explain: The moon gives out no light of its own. It is seen because it reflects light from the sun.
questions.lo: Classify objects as luminous or non-luminous

notes.0: A lit candle flame produces its own light, so it is a light source. Look for the object that only reflects light from somewhere else.
notes.1: A switched-on lamp produces its own light, so it is a light source. Look for the object that only reflects light from another source.
notes.2: The sun produces its own light, so it is a light source. Look for the object that shines only because light from elsewhere falls on it.

why.right: The moon is non-luminous because it shines only by reflecting light from the sun.
wrong: The moon is non-luminous because it gives out only a weak light of its own.
The moon is non-luminous because it can be seen only at night.

questions.q: Which of these emits its own light?
questions.explain: A lit mobile phone screen produces its own light, so it is luminous. A book, a white ball and a plane mirror only reflect light.
questions.lo: Classify objects as luminous or non-luminous

notes.0: A book is seen only because light from a lamp or the sun reflects off its pages. It gives out no light of its own.
notes.1: A white ball looks bright because it reflects most of the light that falls on it. It does not produce light itself.
notes.3: A plane mirror reflects light very well, so it can look bright. It still gives out no light of its own.

why.right: A lit phone screen gives out light because electrical energy is converted into light energy in the screen.
wrong: A lit phone screen gives out light because it reflects the light in the room back out.
A lit phone screen gives out light because its glass stores daylight and releases it slowly.

questions.q: Which object is seen only because it reflects light?
questions.explain: A plane mirror gives out no light of its own. It is seen only because light from other sources reflects off it.
questions.lo: Classify objects as luminous or non-luminous

notes.0: A candle flame produces its own light, so it is seen by the light it gives out. Look for an object that has no light of its own.
notes.2: The sun produces its own light. Look for an object that would not be seen if no light from other sources fell on it.
notes.3: A firefly makes its own light, so it can be seen in the dark. Look for an object that gives out no light at all.

why.right: A plane mirror is non-luminous, so it is seen only when light from a source reflects off it into the eye.
wrong: A plane mirror is luminous, so it is seen by the faint light it gives out on its own.
A plane mirror is non-luminous, so it is seen by light that travels out from the eye to the mirror.

questions.q: The bouncing of light off a surface is called
questions.explain: Reflection is the bouncing of light off a surface, such as a mirror.
questions.lo: Explain how we see objects using reflection

notes.0: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its colours. Bouncing off a surface does not split light into colours.
notes.1: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes into a different material. Here the light does not enter the material but comes back off it.
notes.2: In absorption the light is taken in by the surface and does not come back off it. Here the light comes back off the surface.

questions.q: We see a non-luminous object when light
choices: reflects off it into our eyes
travels from our eyes to it
questions.explain: A non-luminous object gives out no light. We see it when light from a source reflects off the object and enters our eyes.
questions.lo: Explain how we see objects using reflection

notes.0: Light that passes around an object does not come from the object, so it cannot show the object to us. Think about where light must go after reaching the object.
notes.2: Eyes do not send out light. They only receive light, so think about which way light must travel for an object to be seen.
notes.3: Light that is absorbed by an object does not leave it, so it cannot reach the eye. Some light must come back off the object.

why.right: A non-luminous object is seen when light bouncing off it enters the eye.
wrong: A non-luminous object is seen when light sent out by the eye reaches it.
A non-luminous object is seen when it soaks up light and then glows.

questions.q: A white ball and a black ball are in a totally dark room. Which is seen?
questions.explain: Neither ball gives out its own light. In a totally dark room there is no light to reflect off them into our eyes, so neither ball is seen.
questions.lo: Explain how we see objects using reflection

notes.1: A black ball absorbs most light, so it would be the harder one to see. In total darkness, think about whether there is any light to reflect at all.
notes.2: Both balls are non-luminous. Think about what must fall on a non-luminous object before it can be seen, and whether this room has any.
notes.3: A white ball reflects light well, but it does not make its own light. Think about what a white surface needs before it can reflect anything.

why.right: In a totally dark room no light falls on either ball, so no light reflects into the eyes.
wrong: In a totally dark room the white ball gives out a faint glow of its own that the eyes can detect.
In a totally dark room the eyes send out enough light to show objects close by.

questions.q: The line perpendicular to the mirror at the point of incidence is the
questions.explain: The normal is a line drawn at 90° to the mirror at the point where the ray hits it. Angles in ray diagrams are measured from it.
questions.lo: Name the parts of a reflection ray diagram

notes.0: The incident ray is the ray of light travelling towards the mirror. The line in the question is a construction line drawn at 90° to the mirror.
notes.1: The boundary is the surface of the mirror itself. The line in the question is at 90° to that surface, so it has a different name.
notes.3: The reflected ray is the ray of light leaving the mirror. The line in the question is a construction line at 90° to the mirror, not a ray.

questions.q: The ray of light hitting a reflecting surface is the
questions.explain: The incident ray is the ray of light travelling towards a surface and hitting it.
questions.lo: Name the parts of a reflection ray diagram

notes.0: A refracted ray is one that has passed into a new material and changed direction. The ray here has not reached the surface yet.
notes.2: The normal is a construction line at 90° to the surface, not a ray of light. The question asks about the light arriving at the surface.
notes.3: The reflected ray is the one leaving the surface after bouncing off. The question asks about the ray before it reaches the surface.

questions.q: The ray travelling away from a surface after bouncing off it is the
questions.explain: The reflected ray is the ray that travels away from the surface after the light bounces off it.
questions.lo: Name the parts of a reflection ray diagram

notes.1: The normal is a construction line at 90° to the surface, not a ray of light. The question asks about light leaving the surface.
notes.2: A refracted ray passes into a new material and bends. Light that bounces back off a surface does not enter the material.
notes.3: The incident ray is the one arriving at the surface. The question asks about the ray after it has bounced off.

questions.q: The angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the
questions.explain: The angle of incidence is measured between the incident ray and the normal, not between the ray and the mirror surface.
questions.lo: Name the parts of a reflection ray diagram

notes.0: Angles in ray diagrams are not measured from the horizontal, since a mirror can be tilted. They are measured from a line drawn at the point of incidence.
notes.1: The angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray is made of two angles added together. The angle of incidence is only one of them.
notes.2: The angle between the ray and the mirror surface is not the angle of incidence. Angles in ray diagrams are measured from a line at 90° to the mirror.

questions.q: The angle between the reflected ray and the normal is the
questions.explain: The angle of reflection is the angle between the reflected ray and the normal.
questions.lo: Name the parts of a reflection ray diagram

notes.0: The angle of refraction is used when light passes into a new material and bends. The reflected ray bounces back and stays in the same material.
notes.1: A right angle is any angle of 90°. The angle between the reflected ray and the normal can be any size, so it has its own name.
notes.3: The angle of incidence belongs to the incident ray, the ray arriving at the surface. The question asks about the ray leaving the surface.

questions.q: For reflection, the angle of reflection is
choices: smaller than the angle of incidence
equal to the angle of incidence
greater than the angle of incidence
questions.explain: The law of reflection states that the angle of reflection is always equal to the angle of incidence.
questions.lo: Apply angle of reflection equals angle of incidence

notes.0: Reflection does not shrink the angle. Look at a ray diagram and compare the angles on each side of the normal using the law of reflection.
notes.1: The angle of reflection is not fixed. It changes whenever the angle of incidence changes, so think about how the two angles are linked.
notes.3: Reflection does not widen the angle. Compare the angle of the incoming ray and the angle of the outgoing ray, both measured from the normal.

questions.q: The angle of incidence is 30°. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explain: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. The angle of incidence is 30°, so the angle of reflection is also 30°.
questions.lo: Apply angle of reflection equals angle of incidence

notes.0: 90° is the angle between the normal and the mirror, not the angle of the reflected ray. Use the law of reflection to link the two angles.
notes.1: Halving the angle of incidence gives 15°, but reflection does not halve the angle. Use the law of reflection to link the two angles.
notes.2: 60° is the angle between the incident ray and the mirror, found by taking 30° from 90°. The angle of reflection is measured from the normal.

why.right: The law of reflection states that the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
wrong: The law of reflection states that the angle of reflection and the angle of incidence add up to 90°.
The law of reflection states that the angle of reflection is half the angle of incidence.

questions.q: The angle of incidence is 45°. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explain: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so an angle of incidence of 45° gives an angle of reflection of 45°.
questions.lo: Apply angle of reflection equals angle of incidence

notes.1: 135° is found by taking 45° from 180°. Angles of reflection are measured from the normal and are never more than 90°.
notes.2: Halving the angle of incidence gives 22.5°, but reflection does not halve the angle. Use the law of reflection to link the two angles.
notes.3: 90° is the total angle between the incident ray and the reflected ray here, not the angle of reflection alone. Each angle is measured from the normal.

why.right: The reflected ray makes the same angle with the normal as the incident ray does.
wrong: The reflected ray makes half the angle with the normal that the incident ray does.
The reflected ray makes an angle with the normal that adds up to 180° with the incident angle.

questions.q: A ray hits a mirror along the normal. What is the angle of reflection?
questions.explain: A ray along the normal has an angle of incidence of 0°. The angle of reflection equals this, so it is 0° and the ray reflects straight back.
questions.lo: Apply angle of reflection equals angle of incidence

notes.0: The ray makes 90° with the mirror surface, but angles are measured from the normal. Work out the angle between this ray and the normal first.
notes.2: 45° would need the ray to arrive at a slant to the normal. This ray lies along the normal, so find its angle of incidence first.
notes.3: 180° describes the ray turning round to go back, but angles of reflection are measured from the normal. Find the angle of incidence first.

why.right: A ray along the normal has an angle of incidence of 0°, so it reflects straight back along the normal.
wrong: A ray along the normal has an angle of incidence of 90°, so it reflects along the mirror surface.
A ray along the normal has an angle of incidence of 0°, so it passes straight through the mirror.

questions.q: The angle of reflection is 25°. What is the angle of incidence?
questions.explain: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, so if the angle of reflection is 25°, the angle of incidence is also 25°.
questions.lo: Apply angle of reflection equals angle of incidence

notes.0: Doubling the angle gives 50°, which is the total angle between the two rays. Each angle is measured separately from the normal.
notes.2: 155° is found by taking 25° from 180°. Angles of incidence are measured from the normal and are never more than 90°.
notes.3: 65° is the angle between the reflected ray and the mirror, found by taking 25° from 90°. The angle of incidence is measured from the normal.

why.right: The law of reflection works both ways, so the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.
wrong: The law of reflection works both ways, so the angle of incidence is double the angle of reflection.
The law of reflection works both ways, so the two angles always add up to 90°.

questions.q: A ray makes 60° with the mirror surface. What is the angle of incidence?
questions.explain: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror. So the angle of incidence is 90° minus 60°, which is 30°.
questions.lo: Apply angle of reflection equals angle of incidence

notes.1: 90° is the angle between the normal and the mirror. The angle of incidence is the angle between the ray and the normal.
notes.2: 120° is found by taking 60° from 180°. The angle of incidence lies between the ray and the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror.
notes.3: 60° is the angle from the mirror surface. The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror.

why.right: The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, which is at 90° to the mirror surface.
wrong: The angle of incidence is measured from the mirror surface, which is where the ray strikes.
The angle of incidence is measured from the reflected ray, which leaves the mirror at the same point.

questions.q: An image in a plane mirror is
questions.explain: A plane mirror forms an image that is upright, the same size as the object, virtual and laterally inverted.
questions.lo: State and apply the characteristics of a plane mirror image

notes.0: A person's head appears at the top of their image in a plane mirror. Check which way up the image is, not just its size.
notes.1: A plane mirror image is neither upside down nor smaller. Think about how a reflection in a bathroom mirror looks compared with the real person.
notes.2: A plane mirror does not enlarge the image. Magnified images come from a concave mirror used close up, so think again about the size of a plane mirror image.

questions.q: A virtual image is one that
choices: cannot be formed on a screen
can be formed on a screen
questions.explain: A virtual image cannot be formed on a screen because the light rays do not actually meet where the image appears.
questions.lo: State and apply the characteristics of a plane mirror image

notes.0: Size is not what makes an image virtual. A virtual image can be larger, smaller or the same size as the object.
notes.1: Being upside down is not what makes an image virtual. The image in a plane mirror is virtual and upright.
notes.3: An image that can be caught on a screen is called a real image. Think about whether light actually reaches the place where a virtual image appears.

questions.q: A plane mirror reversing left and right is called
questions.explain: Lateral inversion is the reversal of left and right in the image formed by a plane mirror.
questions.lo: State and apply the characteristics of a plane mirror image

notes.0: Magnification is a change in the size of an image. A plane mirror image is the same size, but its left and right sides are swapped.
notes.1: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into colours by a prism. It has nothing to do with swapping left and right.
notes.2: Refraction is the bending of light when it passes into a new material. A mirror reflects light instead.

questions.q: A girl stands 2 m from a plane mirror. How far is her image from the mirror?
questions.explain: In a plane mirror the image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front. The girl is 2 m in front, so her image is 2 m behind.
questions.lo: State and apply the characteristics of a plane mirror image

notes.0: The image is not on the mirror surface. It appears behind the mirror, at a distance linked to how far the object is in front.
notes.2: Halving the distance gives 1 m, but the image is not closer to the mirror than the object. Compare the two distances from the mirror.
notes.3: 4 m is the distance between the girl and her image. The question asks only for the distance from the image to the mirror.

why.right: A plane mirror image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.
wrong: A plane mirror image is half as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.
A plane mirror image is twice as far behind the mirror as the object is in front of it.

questions.q: A boy stands 1.5 m from a plane mirror. How far is he from his image?
questions.explain: The image is 1.5 m behind the mirror and the boy is 1.5 m in front of it. The distance between them is 1.5 m + 1.5 m = 3 m.
questions.lo: State and apply the characteristics of a plane mirror image

notes.0: 6 m is four times the distance to the mirror. The image is only as far behind the mirror as the boy is in front.
notes.1: Halving gives 0.75 m, but the image is not closer than the boy. Add the distance of the boy in front to the distance of the image behind.
notes.3: 1.5 m is the distance from the boy to the mirror. The question asks for the distance from the boy to his image, which is behind the mirror.

why.right: The image is as far behind the mirror as the boy is in front, so the two distances are added.
wrong: The image is formed on the mirror surface, so the distance is just the distance of the boy from the mirror.
The image is twice as far behind the mirror as the boy is in front, so the distance is doubled.

questions.q: A cat is 6 m from its image in a plane mirror. How far is it from the mirror?
questions.explain: The cat and its image are the same distance from the mirror. The 6 m between them is split equally, so the cat is 3 m from the mirror.
questions.lo: State and apply the characteristics of a plane mirror image

notes.1: Dividing by three gives 2 m, but the gap has only two parts, one in front of the mirror and one behind. Compare those two parts.
notes.2: 6 m is the distance between the cat and its image. The mirror lies somewhere between them.
notes.3: Doubling gives 12 m, but the distance from the cat to the mirror is only part of the 6 m gap, not more than it.

why.right: In a plane mirror, the mirror lies halfway between the object and its image.
wrong: In a plane mirror, the mirror lies one third of the way from the object to its image.
In a plane mirror, the mirror lies at the image, because the image forms on its surface.

questions.q: You raise your right hand in front of a plane mirror. Your image raises its
questions.explain: A plane mirror image is laterally inverted, so left and right are reversed. When the right hand is raised, the image raises its left hand.
questions.lo: State and apply the characteristics of a plane mirror image

notes.1: The image faces the person, so its sides are swapped compared with the person. Think about lateral inversion in a plane mirror.
notes.2: A mirror does not add a second raised hand. The image copies the one movement with a change, so think about lateral inversion.

why.right: A plane mirror image is laterally inverted, so the left and right sides are swapped.
wrong: A plane mirror image is upside down, so the left and right sides are swapped.
A plane mirror image is formed by refraction, so the left and right sides are swapped.

questions.q: Why is "AMBULANCE" printed in reverse on the front of an ambulance?
choices: it can be seen at night
it is larger in a mirror
it reads correctly in a driver's mirror
questions.explain: A plane mirror laterally inverts writing. Printing the word AMBULANCE in reverse means it reads the right way round in the mirror of the driver in front.
questions.lo: State and apply the characteristics of a plane mirror image

notes.0: Reversing the letters does not make them brighter or easier to see in the dark. Think about how the word looks in a mirror.
notes.1: A plane mirror image is the same size as the object, so reversing the letters cannot make them larger. Think about lateral inversion.
notes.3: Reversing the letters does not change their colour. Think about what a mirror does to left and right in writing.

why.right: A rear-view mirror laterally inverts writing, so reversed letters appear the right way round.
wrong: A rear-view mirror magnifies writing, so reversed letters appear larger and clearer.
A rear-view mirror turns writing upside down, so reversed letters appear upright.

questions.q: A convex mirror forms an image that is
questions.explain: A convex mirror curves outwards. It forms an image that is upright and smaller than the object, which gives a wide view.
questions.lo: Choose a plane, convex or concave mirror for a given use

notes.0: An upright, magnified image comes from a concave mirror used close up. A convex mirror curves outwards and shows a wide view, so think about image size.
notes.1: A same-size image comes from a plane mirror. A convex mirror curves outwards and fits a wide view into a small space.
notes.2: A convex mirror does not form an upside-down image. Think about how things look in a mirror at a road junction.

questions.q: A concave mirror used close up forms an image that is
questions.explain: When an object is close to a concave mirror, the image is upright and magnified. This is why concave mirrors are used as make-up and dental mirrors.
questions.lo: Choose a plane, convex or concave mirror for a given use

notes.0: An upright, smaller image comes from a convex mirror. A concave mirror used close up is chosen for seeing fine detail.
notes.2: A concave mirror can form an inverted image, but only when the object is far away. This question is about an object close to the mirror.
notes.3: A same-size image comes from a plane mirror. A concave mirror used close up is chosen for seeing fine detail, such as in make-up mirrors.

questions.q: Which mirror is used at road junctions to see around blind corners?
questions.explain: A convex mirror gives an upright, diminished image with a wide field of view, so drivers can see more of the road around a blind corner.
questions.lo: Choose a plane, convex or concave mirror for a given use

notes.0: A plane mirror shows only a narrow view at the same size as the scene. Around a blind corner, drivers need to see as much of the road as possible.
notes.1: A concave mirror gives a magnified view of things close to it, which shows only a small area. Drivers at a corner need a wide view.

why.right: Road junction mirrors are convex because they give a wide field of view.
wrong: Road junction mirrors are convex because they give a magnified image of cars.
Road junction mirrors are convex because they give an image the same size as the cars.

questions.q: Which mirror does a dentist use to examine teeth closely?
questions.explain: A concave mirror held close to a tooth forms an upright, magnified image, so the dentist can see small details clearly.
questions.lo: Choose a plane, convex or concave mirror for a given use

notes.1: A convex mirror makes things look smaller to give a wide view. A dentist needs to see the small details of one tooth.
notes.2: A plane mirror shows the tooth at the same size. A dentist needs the details of the tooth to look larger.

why.right: Dental mirrors are concave because they form an upright, magnified image when held close.
wrong: Dental mirrors are concave because they form an upright, diminished image with a wide view.
Dental mirrors are concave because they form an image that is not laterally inverted.

questions.q: Which mirror is used in a periscope?
questions.explain: A periscope uses two plane mirrors. They reflect light along the tube and give an upright image that is the same size as the view.
questions.lo: Choose a plane, convex or concave mirror for a given use

notes.0: A convex mirror makes the view smaller and harder to judge. A periscope needs to show the scene at its true size.
notes.2: A concave mirror magnifies only nearby objects and can turn distant images upside down. A periscope shows a distant scene the right way up at true size.

why.right: Periscopes use plane mirrors because these give an upright image the same size as the object.
wrong: Periscopes use plane mirrors because these bend light as it passes through the glass.
Periscopes use plane mirrors because these magnify distant objects so they look closer.

questions.q: Which mirror is used in car headlights to form a strong beam?
questions.explain: A concave mirror behind the bulb reflects the light forward into a strong, narrow beam instead of letting it spread out.
questions.lo: Choose a plane, convex or concave mirror for a given use

notes.1: A plane mirror reflects light without bringing the rays together, so the light keeps spreading out. A headlight needs the rays sent forward together.
notes.2: A convex mirror spreads reflected light out over a wide area. A headlight needs the light sent forward in one strong beam.

why.right: Headlight mirrors are concave because they reflect the light of the bulb forward in a narrow, strong beam.
wrong: Headlight mirrors are concave because they spread the light of the bulb out over a wide area.
Headlight mirrors are concave because they produce extra light of their own.

questions.q: A mirror forms an upright, magnified image of a face. Which mirror is it?
questions.explain: Only a concave mirror held close to the face forms an upright, magnified image. This is how a make-up mirror works.
questions.lo: Choose a plane, convex or concave mirror for a given use

notes.0: A plane mirror forms an upright image, but it is the same size as the face, not magnified.
notes.2: A convex mirror forms an upright image, but it is smaller than the face, not magnified.

why.right: A concave mirror forms an upright, magnified image when an object is close to it.
wrong: A concave mirror forms an upright, same-size image of any object placed in front of it.
A concave mirror forms an upright, magnified image of any object, however far away it is.

questions.q: Parallel rays falling on a smooth surface are reflected
questions.explain: A smooth surface is flat, so parallel rays all meet it at the same angle of incidence. The rays are reflected in the same direction.
questions.lo: Compare reflection on smooth and rough surfaces

notes.0: Reflection sends light back off a surface, not into it. Think about the direction the rays take after they bounce.
notes.1: Rays reflect back along the normal only when they arrive along it. These parallel rays can arrive at any angle.
notes.2: Rays go off in different directions from a rough surface, where the normals point different ways. A smooth surface has the same normal everywhere.

why.right: On a smooth surface, the normals are all parallel, so every ray reflects at the same angle.
wrong: On a smooth surface, less light is absorbed, so every ray reflects in the same direction.
On a smooth surface, the rays all reflect along the normal, so they leave in the same direction.

questions.q: Parallel rays falling on a rough surface are reflected
questions.explain: A rough surface has tiny bumps facing different ways, so the normals point in different directions. Parallel rays are reflected in different directions.
questions.lo: Compare reflection on smooth and rough surfaces

notes.0: Parallel rays leave in the same direction only from a smooth, flat surface. A rough surface has tiny bumps that face different ways.
notes.1: Rays reflect back along the normal only when they arrive along it. On a rough surface, think about how the bumps change the normal at each point.
notes.2: Reflection sends light back off a surface, not into it. Think about how tiny bumps affect the direction of each reflected ray.

why.right: On a rough surface, the normal points a different way at each point, so rays reflect in different directions.
wrong: On a rough surface, the law of reflection does not apply, so rays reflect in different directions.
On a rough surface, some rays slow down more than others, so rays reflect in different directions.

questions.q: For a rough surface, the angle of reflection of each ray is
choices: larger than its angle of incidence
equal to its angle of incidence
smaller than its angle of incidence
questions.explain: The law of reflection applies to every ray, even on a rough surface. Each ray reflects at an angle equal to its own angle of incidence.
questions.lo: Compare reflection on smooth and rough surfaces

notes.0: An angle of reflection of zero happens only for a ray arriving along the normal. On a rough surface rays arrive at many different angles.
notes.1: A rough surface does not change the law of reflection. It only changes the direction of the normal at each point.
notes.3: A rough surface does not make angles of reflection smaller. The bumps only change which way the normal points at each point.

why.right: Every ray obeys the law of reflection, but the normal points a different way at each bump.
wrong: Every ray slows down at a rough surface, so it leaves at a different angle from how it arrived.
Every ray loses some energy at a rough surface, so its angle of reflection changes.

questions.q: Why can we not see our reflection on white paper?
questions.explain: Paper has a rough surface, so it reflects light in many different directions. The reflected rays do not form a clear image.
questions.lo: Compare reflection on smooth and rough surfaces

notes.0: Paper that absorbed all light would look black. White paper reflects most light, so think about the directions the reflected light takes.
notes.1: Paper does not give out its own light, so it is non-luminous. Think about how the shape of its surface affects reflection.
notes.2: Light that hits paper mostly bounces off rather than passing into it. Think about how the surface affects the directions of the reflected rays.

why.right: White paper reflects light in many directions, so rays from one point do not stay together to form an image.
wrong: White paper reflects light too weakly, so too little light reaches the eye to form an image.
White paper does not obey the law of reflection, so its reflected rays cannot form an image.

questions.q: On which surface will a clear image form?
questions.explain: Calm water has a smooth, flat surface. Parallel rays reflect off it in the same direction, so a clear image forms.
questions.lo: Compare reflection on smooth and rough surfaces

notes.0: Paper looks smooth, but its surface is rough at a small scale. It reflects light in many directions, so no clear image forms.
notes.2: A wooden table has a rough surface unless it is highly polished. Look for the surface that is the smoothest and flattest.
notes.3: A brick wall is very rough, so it reflects light in many directions. Look for the surface that is the smoothest and flattest.

why.right: Calm water is smooth and flat, so parallel rays reflect off it in the same direction.
wrong: Calm water is transparent, so light passes through it and forms an image underneath.
Calm water is dark in colour, so it absorbs light and shows the image clearly.

questions.q: The bending of light at the boundary between two transparent materials is
questions.explain: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent material into another, such as from air into water.
questions.lo: Explain refraction as a change in the speed of light

notes.1: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into colours. Light bending at any boundary between two materials has a more general name.
notes.2: Reflection is light bouncing back off a surface. Here the light passes through the boundary into the second material.
notes.3: In absorption, light is taken in by a material and does not come out. Here the light carries on through the boundary.

questions.q: Refraction happens because light
questions.explain: Light travels at different speeds in different materials. When it crosses a boundary at an angle, the change in speed makes it bend.
questions.lo: Explain refraction as a change in the speed of light

notes.0: Absorbed light does not travel on, so it cannot bend. Refraction happens to light that passes through into the new material.
notes.1: Light keeps its colour when it passes from one material into another. Think about what else is different for light in each material.
notes.3: Light that stopped at the boundary would not pass into the second material. In refraction, light carries on through but in a new direction.

why.right: Light bends at a boundary because one side of the beam changes speed before the other side.
wrong: Light bends at a boundary because the second material pulls the light towards it.
Light bends at a boundary because some of the light is absorbed at the surface.

questions.q: The more optically dense a material is, the
questions.explain: Optical density describes how much a material slows light down. The more optically dense the material, the slower light travels in it.
questions.lo: Explain refraction as a change in the speed of light

notes.1: Optical density is not about mass. It describes how a material affects light, which is different from how heavy the material is.
notes.2: This is the reverse of the idea. Think about light entering glass from air, and whether it speeds up or slows down.
notes.3: Optical density does not change how bright light is. It is about how the material affects light travelling through it.

questions.q: Light travels from air into glass. It
choices: slows down and bends away from the normal
speeds up and bends away from the normal
slows down and bends towards the normal
speeds up and bends towards the normal
questions.explain: Glass is optically denser than air, so light slows down when it enters glass. This makes it bend towards the normal.
questions.lo: Predict whether light bends towards or away from the normal

notes.0: Light does slow down in glass, but slowing down is linked to one direction of bending. Check which way a slower ray turns relative to the normal.
notes.1: Glass is optically denser than air, so light does not speed up when entering it. Both the speed change and the bending need checking.
notes.3: Glass is optically denser than air. Think about what that means for the speed of light inside the glass.

why.right: Light bends towards the normal entering glass because it slows down in the optically denser material.
wrong: Light bends towards the normal entering glass because the normal attracts light that hits the glass.
Light bends towards the normal entering glass because it speeds up in the optically denser material.

questions.q: Light travels from glass into air. It
choices: speeds up and bends towards the normal
slows down and bends away from the normal
slows down and bends towards the normal
speeds up and bends away from the normal
questions.explain: Air is less optically dense than glass, so light speeds up when it leaves glass. This makes it bend away from the normal.
questions.lo: Predict whether light bends towards or away from the normal

notes.0: Light does speed up in air, but speeding up is linked to one direction of bending. Check which way a faster ray turns relative to the normal.
notes.1: Air is less optically dense than glass. Think about what that means for the speed of light once it is in the air.
notes.2: Air is less optically dense than glass, so light does not slow down when it enters air. Both the speed change and the bending need checking.

why.right: Light bends away from the normal leaving glass because it speeds up in the less optically dense air.
wrong: Light bends away from the normal leaving glass because it slows down in the less optically dense air.
Light bends away from the normal leaving glass because the glass surface pushes the light outwards.

questions.q: Light travels from air into water at an angle. It bends
questions.explain: Water is optically denser than air, so light slows down as it enters water at an angle and bends towards the normal.
questions.lo: Predict whether light bends towards or away from the normal

notes.0: Bending away from the normal happens when light speeds up. Think about whether light speeds up or slows down when it enters water.
notes.2: Light that goes back into the air has been reflected, not refracted. This question is about light passing into the water.
notes.3: Light entering water does not run along the surface. It passes into the water, so think about how its speed changes there.

why.right: Light slows down when it enters water from air, so it bends towards the normal.
wrong: Light speeds up when it enters water from air, so it bends towards the normal.
Light is pulled down by the weight of the water, so it bends towards the normal.

questions.q: Light travels from water into air at an angle. It bends
questions.explain: Air is less optically dense than water, so light speeds up as it leaves water at an angle and bends away from the normal.
questions.lo: Predict whether light bends towards or away from the normal

notes.0: Bending towards the normal happens when light slows down. Think about whether light speeds up or slows down when it enters air from water.
notes.1: Light passing from water into air does not run along the surface. It enters the air, so think about how its speed changes there.
notes.3: Light that goes back into the water has been reflected, not refracted. This question is about light passing into the air.

why.right: Light speeds up when it enters air from water, so it bends away from the normal.
wrong: Light slows down when it enters air from water, so it bends away from the normal.
Light is pulled up by the lighter air above, so it bends away from the normal.

questions.q: Light enters a block along the normal. What happens to its direction?
choices: it bends away from the normal
questions.explain: A ray along the normal meets the boundary straight on. Its speed changes, but its direction does not, so it passes straight through.
questions.lo: Predict whether light bends towards or away from the normal

notes.0: A ray can only bend towards the normal if it arrives at an angle to it. This ray already travels along the normal.
notes.1: A ray can only bend away from the normal if it arrives at an angle to it. This ray already travels along the normal.
notes.2: The block is transparent, so the light passes into it. The question is about the direction of the light inside the block.

why.right: A ray along the normal changes speed but not direction, since it meets the boundary straight on.
wrong: A ray along the normal does not change speed, since it meets the boundary straight on.
A ray along the normal changes speed but not direction, since the block is too thin to bend it.

questions.q: A ray bends towards the normal entering material X from air. Light in X is
choices: the same speed as in air
questions.explain: Light bends towards the normal when it slows down. So material X is optically denser than air, and light is slower in X.
questions.lo: Predict whether light bends towards or away from the normal

notes.1: Light that stopped completely could not form a ray inside X. The ray carries on in X, so think about how its speed changed.
notes.2: Light that speeds up bends away from the normal. Link the direction of bending to the change in speed.
notes.3: If the speed stayed the same, the ray would not bend at all. The ray did bend, so its speed must have changed.

why.right: Light bends towards the normal only when it slows down on entering the new material.
wrong: Light bends towards the normal only when it speeds up on entering the new material.
Light bends towards the normal only when the new material is heavier than air.

questions.q: A pencil in a glass of water appears bent because of
questions.explain: Light from the part of the pencil under water bends as it passes from water into air. This makes that part appear in a different place.
questions.lo: Describe effects of refraction in everyday life

notes.0: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. Here the light from the pencil passes from water into air, crossing a boundary.
notes.2: Dispersion splits white light into colours. The pencil does not show colours. It looks bent, so think about light crossing from water into air.
notes.3: Lateral inversion is the swap of left and right in a plane mirror. There is no mirror here, only light passing from water into air.

why.right: A pencil in water looks bent because light from the pencil changes direction as it leaves the water.
wrong: A pencil in water looks bent because the water splits the light from the pencil into colours.
A pencil in water looks bent because light from the pencil reflects off the water surface.

questions.q: Due to refraction, a swimming pool appears
questions.explain: Light from the bottom of the pool bends away from the normal as it leaves the water. The bottom appears raised, so the pool looks shallower than it is.
questions.lo: Describe effects of refraction in everyday life

notes.0: Light from the bottom bends as it leaves the water, so the pool does not look its true depth. Think about where the bottom appears to be.
notes.1: Light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it enters the air. Trace the rays back to see whether the bottom appears higher or lower.
notes.2: Refraction at the surface mainly changes how deep things look. Think about whether the bottom appears higher or lower than it really is.

why.right: A pool looks shallower because light from the bottom bends away from the normal as it leaves the water.
wrong: A pool looks shallower because light from the bottom bends towards the normal as it leaves the water.
A pool looks shallower because light from the bottom reflects off the water surface back down.

questions.q: Letters under a glass block appear
choices: further from the surface than they are
nearer to the surface than they are
questions.explain: Light from the letters bends away from the normal as it leaves the glass. The letters appear raised, nearer to the surface than they really are.
questions.lo: Describe effects of refraction in everyday life

notes.0: A glass block does not turn letters upside down. Refraction at the top surface changes how deep the letters appear.
notes.1: Light from the letters bends away from the normal as it leaves the glass. Trace the rays back to see whether the letters appear raised or lowered.
notes.3: Lateral inversion happens in a plane mirror. A glass block refracts light, which changes how deep the letters appear.

why.right: Letters under glass look raised because their light bends away from the normal as it leaves the glass.
wrong: Letters under glass look raised because their light bends towards the normal as it leaves the glass.
Letters under glass look raised because the glass reflects their light back up from the bottom.

questions.q: Which is an effect of refraction?
choices: a coin in water looks nearer the surface
seeing your face in a mirror
questions.explain: Light from the coin bends as it passes from water into air, so the coin appears nearer the surface. The other options are caused by straight-line travel or reflection.
questions.lo: Describe effects of refraction in everyday life

notes.0: A shadow forms because light travels in straight lines and is blocked. No light crosses a boundary between materials here.
notes.2: The moon is seen because it reflects sunlight. Refraction needs light to cross a boundary between two transparent materials.
notes.3: A face in a mirror is seen by reflection, which is light bouncing off a surface. Refraction needs light to pass into a different material.

why.right: A coin in water looks nearer the surface because its light bends as it passes from water into air.
wrong: A coin in water looks nearer the surface because its light bounces off the water surface.
A coin in water looks nearer the surface because the water splits its light into colours.

questions.q: The splitting of white light into its colours is called
questions.explain: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into its seven colours, for example by a prism.
questions.lo: Describe dispersion of white light by a prism

notes.1: Reflection is light bouncing off a surface. It does not separate white light into colours.
notes.2: Lateral inversion is the swap of left and right in a plane mirror image. It has nothing to do with colours.
notes.3: In absorption, light is taken in by a material. Splitting white light into colours has a different name.

questions.q: How many colours make up white light?
questions.explain: White light is made up of seven colours. They are red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet.
questions.lo: Describe dispersion of white light by a prism

notes.0: Six colours leaves one out. Count the colours of the spectrum in order from red to violet, including indigo.
notes.1: Five colours leaves some out. Count the colours of the spectrum in order from red to violet.
notes.3: Three colours leaves most of the spectrum out. Count the colours from red to violet, as seen in a rainbow.

questions.q: White light passes through a prism. Which colour bends the most?
questions.explain: Violet light slows down the most in glass, so it is refracted through the largest angle.
questions.lo: Describe dispersion of white light by a prism

notes.0: Yellow lies near the middle of the spectrum, so its bending is in between. Look at the end of the spectrum that bends the most.
notes.2: Red is at the end of the spectrum that bends the least. Look at the other end of the spectrum.
notes.3: Green lies near the middle of the spectrum, so its bending is in between. Look at the end of the spectrum that bends the most.

why.right: Violet bends the most because it slows down more than any other colour in glass.
wrong: Violet bends the most because it travels faster than any other colour in glass.
Violet bends the most because it is reflected more strongly by the glass surface.

questions.q: White light passes through a prism. Which colour bends the least?
questions.explain: Red light slows down the least in glass, so it is refracted the least.
questions.lo: Describe dispersion of white light by a prism

notes.1: Violet is at the end of the spectrum that bends the most. Look at the other end of the spectrum.
notes.2: Green lies near the middle of the spectrum, so its bending is in between. Look at the end of the spectrum that bends the least.
notes.3: Blue is near the end of the spectrum that bends the most. Look at the end of the spectrum that bends the least.

why.right: Red bends the least because it slows down less than any other colour in glass.
wrong: Red bends the least because it slows down more than any other colour in glass.
Red bends the least because it is the weakest colour and loses its energy in the glass.

questions.q: A prism splits white light because each colour
choices: travels at the same speed in glass
travels at a different speed in glass
questions.explain: Each colour travels at a different speed in glass, so each is refracted by a different amount. The colours spread out into a spectrum.
questions.lo: Describe dispersion of white light by a prism

notes.0: Absorbed light would not come out of the prism. All seven colours come out, so think about how each colour behaves inside the glass.
notes.1: The colours come out through the far side of the prism, so they pass through it. Think about how each colour behaves inside the glass.
notes.2: If every colour travelled at the same speed in glass, all would bend by the same amount and stay together as white light.

why.right: Each colour bends by a different amount because the change in speed decides how much light bends.
wrong: Each colour bends by a different amount because the glass absorbs some colours and lets others through.
Each colour bends by a different amount because the prism adds colour to the white light.

questions.q: Which type of EM radiation can we see?
questions.explain: Visible light is the only part of the electromagnetic spectrum that human eyes can detect.
questions.lo: State beneficial and harmful effects of infrared, UV and visible light

notes.0: UV radiation cannot be detected by the human eye, even though it comes with sunlight. It is noticed by its effects, such as sunburn.
notes.2: Infrared radiation cannot be seen by the human eye. It is felt as heat on the skin.

questions.q: Thermal imaging cameras screen people for fever by detecting
questions.explain: All warm objects give out infrared radiation, and hotter objects give out more. A thermal imaging camera detects this, so a person with a fever shows up as warmer.
questions.lo: State beneficial and harmful effects of infrared, UV and visible light

notes.1: Visible light shows only what a person looks like, not how warm they are. Think about the radiation that warm bodies give out.
notes.2: People do not give out UV radiation. Think about the radiation that warm bodies give out and that is felt as heat.

why.right: Thermal cameras detect infrared because warmer bodies give out more infrared radiation.
wrong: Thermal cameras detect infrared because warmer bodies reflect more visible light.
Thermal cameras detect infrared because warmer bodies give out more UV radiation.

questions.q: Which radiation helps the body produce vitamin D?
questions.explain: UV radiation in sunlight helps the skin make vitamin D, which is needed for healthy bones and teeth.
questions.lo: State beneficial and harmful effects of infrared, UV and visible light

notes.0: Infrared radiation warms the skin but does not help it make vitamin D. Think about the radiation in sunlight that also causes sunburn.
notes.1: Visible light lets us see but does not help the skin make vitamin D. Think about the radiation in sunlight that also causes sunburn.

questions.q: Sunscreen is worn to protect skin from
questions.explain: Too much UV radiation can cause sunburn and skin cancer. Sunscreen absorbs or blocks much of the UV radiation before it reaches the skin.
questions.lo: State beneficial and harmful effects of infrared, UV and visible light

notes.1: Infrared radiation warms the skin, but sunscreen is not mainly for that. Think about the radiation in sunlight that causes sunburn.
notes.2: Visible light lets us see and is not what sunscreen blocks. Think about the radiation in sunlight that causes sunburn.

why.right: Sunscreen is needed because too much UV radiation can cause sunburn and skin cancer.
wrong: Sunscreen is needed because too much infrared radiation can cause sunburn and skin cancer.
Sunscreen is needed because too much UV radiation stops the skin from making vitamin D.

questions.q: Which radiation trapped in the atmosphere contributes to climate change?
questions.explain: The warm Earth gives out infrared radiation. Greenhouse gases trap some of it in the atmosphere, which warms the Earth and contributes to climate change.
questions.lo: State beneficial and harmful effects of infrared, UV and visible light

notes.0: Visible light from the sun mostly passes through the atmosphere. Think about the radiation given out by the warm ground that greenhouse gases trap.
notes.2: UV radiation is linked to sunburn and the ozone layer, not to trapped heat. Think about the radiation that warm objects give out.

why.right: The Earth gives out infrared radiation, and greenhouse gases trap it, which warms the atmosphere.
wrong: The Earth gives out UV radiation, and greenhouse gases trap it, which warms the atmosphere.
The Earth gives out infrared radiation, and the ozone layer traps it, which warms the atmosphere.

questions.q: Which radiation do plants use for photosynthesis?
questions.explain: Plants absorb visible light with chlorophyll and use its energy to make food by photosynthesis.
questions.lo: State beneficial and harmful effects of infrared, UV and visible light

notes.0: Too much UV radiation can damage plant cells. Think about the light that chlorophyll in leaves absorbs to make food.
notes.1: Infrared radiation mainly warms leaves. Think about the light that chlorophyll in leaves absorbs to make food.

questions.q: Too much artificial light in the environment is called
questions.explain: Light pollution is too much artificial light in the environment, such as bright street lamps and buildings lit up at night.
questions.lo: Describe the impact of artificial lighting on society and the environment

notes.0: Climate change is the long-term change in the weather patterns of the Earth. Too much artificial light is a different problem with its own name.
notes.1: Refraction is the bending of light at a boundary between materials. It is a property of light, not an environmental problem.
notes.2: Dispersion is the splitting of white light into colours. It is a property of light, not an environmental problem.

questions.q: How can artificial lighting harm migratory birds?
questions.explain: Migratory birds use natural light cues to know when and where to fly. Artificial light at night can confuse them and disrupt their migration timing.
questions.lo: Describe the impact of artificial lighting on society and the environment

notes.0: The question asks how artificial lighting harms birds, and better vision would not be harm. Think about how birds use natural light to decide when to travel.
notes.1: Helping birds find nests would be a benefit, not harm. Think about how birds use natural light to decide when to travel.
notes.2: Artificial light does not give birds more food, and that would not be harm. Think about how birds use natural light to decide when to travel.

why.right: Bright artificial light at night confuses birds that use natural light cues to time their migration.
wrong: Bright artificial light at night heats the air and makes birds too warm to fly.
Bright artificial light at night blinds birds for good so they cannot see their nests.

questions.q: Which lighting reduces energy use and light pollution?
questions.explain: LEDs use less electrical energy than older lamps for the same amount of light. Using them only where and when needed also reduces light pollution.
questions.lo: Describe the impact of artificial lighting on society and the environment

notes.1: More street lamps would add light and use more energy. Look for an option that cuts both energy use and stray light.
notes.2: Brighter floodlights use more energy and send more light into the sky. Look for an option that cuts both.
notes.3: Lights left on all night waste energy and add to light pollution. Look for an option that uses light only when it is needed.

why.right: LEDs use less energy for the same light, and switching them on only when needed cuts light pollution.
wrong: LEDs give out more light than other lamps, so leaving them on all night cuts light pollution.
LEDs use more energy than other lamps, so they are switched on less often and cut light pollution.
